author: high
claim: The full target follows from two elementary mechanisms: on six vertices, any chosen vertex has three incident edges of one color, forcing either a same-color triangle through that vertex or an opposite-color triangle among the three endpoints; on five vertices, coloring a 5-cycle red and its complementary 5-cycle blue avoids monochromatic triangles.
evidence: For the upper bound, choose a vertex v. Its five incident edges cannot have at most two red and at most two blue edges, so some color C occurs on vx, vy, vz. If one of xy, yz, zx has color C, it and the corresponding two edges to v form a C-colored triangle; if none does, xy, yz, zx all have the other color and form a monochromatic triangle. For the lower bound, label the five vertices 1,2,3,4,5; color 12,23,34,45,51 red and all remaining edges 13,24,35,41,52 blue. The red edges form the cycle 1-2-3-4-5-1, and the blue edges form the cycle 1-3-5-2-4-1. In either cycle, the two same-colored neighbors of any vertex are not joined in that color, so no same-colored triangle exists.

links.statement: Prove that every red-blue coloring of the edges of the complete graph on six vertices contains a monochromatic triangle, while there is a red-blue coloring of the complete graph on five vertices containing no monochromatic triangle. Equivalently, prove that the Ramsey number R(3,3) equals 6.

glossary.v: an arbitrarily selected vertex of the complete graph on six vertices
glossary.x, y, z: three distinct neighbors of v joined to v by edges of the same color
glossary.C: one of the two edge colors
